newsitem.title: USA: Senators assured Conrail breakup means jobs.
newsitem.headline: Senators assured Conrail breakup means jobs.

text.p: The presidents of CSX Corp and Norfolk Southern Corp told worried northeastern senators Thursday a proposed $10.3 billion deal to acquire and divide Conrail Inc meant more jobs.

"We're making a major bet on growth," Norfolk Southern chairman David Goode said, "If we do (grow) it's going to be jobs," just the kind of reassurance senators from Maryland, Pennsylvania and New Jersey said they were looking for at a Senate Appropriations Transportation Subcommittee hearing.
Under an agreement announced March 7, Conrail shareholders would get $115 per share in cash by June 2, permitting CSX and Norfolk Southern to negotiate a division of Conrail's assets.
CSX and Norfolk Southern spokesmen contend the new alignment would set up competition between them at most major ports and markets east of the Mississippi.
Southern senators, like Virginia Republican John Warner and Alabama Republican Richard Shelby, said they were comfortable with that. But not northeastern senators.
"We want to know what this merger means in terms of jobs," said Sen. Barbara Mikulski, a Maryland Democrat. "We're concerned about jobs. I look forward to hearing from our railroad tycoons."

Mikulski, New Jersey Democratic Sen. Frank Lautenberg and Pennsylvania Republican Sen. Arlen Specter grilled Goode and CSX CEO John Snow in detail about the effects of the merger on specific cities, towns and ports.
They won assurances, town by town, city by city and port by port, there would be virtually no jobs lost as CSX and Norfolk Southern divided up the 11,000-mile Conrail system.
Both CEOs said, for example, that the city of Philadelphia, now the headquarters of Conrail, would retain important facilities and the port would get new ones.
Maryland Gov. Parris Glendening told the senators he was ready to welcome Norfolk Southern to his state if it competes with CSX and if jobs are protected.
"We truly do not know if our issues have been adequately and explicitly addressed," he said. "The devil is in the details."
But the two CEOs said negotiations between them are still under way and there are no details yet. Instead, they spoke in broad and glowing terms.

The two CEOS argued if CSX and Norfolk Southern divide Conrail's assets they will be more competitive against the trucking industry, because shippers will be able to expedite cargo through one of two competing railroads instead of moving it more slowly through a series of railroads.

"Trucks have the huge portion of the transportation market and just taking a small portion of that market vastly increases our growth rates on the retail side," said Snow of CSX. "That's the sort of key equation here."
"As we win back more traffic from trucks that means more rail jobs, more crews, more cars to be repaired, more trains to be made up, more signals to be repaired," he said.
